title: Steroid Injections vs Tablets for Arthritis: Benefits and Risks
meta_title: Steroid Injections vs Tablets for Arthritis: UK Guide
meta_description: Compare local steroid injections and tablets for arthritis: realistic pain relief, infection warnings, side effects, aftercare and safe stopping plans.
excerpt: Local joint injections and steroid tablets do different jobs. Compare realistic benefits, systemic risks, urgent warning signs and the questions to ask your team.
direct_answer: A local steroid injection targets a joint or nearby tissue; tablets and muscle injections act more widely. The right choice depends on the diagnosis, treatment goal and your risks. For osteoarthritis, NICE describes injection relief of 2 to 10 weeks. A suddenly hot, swollen or very painful joint needs urgent assessment. Do not change or stop steroid tablets without your prescriber's plan.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: steroid injections vs tablets arthritis, joint injection prednisolone, steroid injection risks, steroid tablets taper, osteoarthritis steroid injection
content:
First check: urgent symptoms are not a routine flare

This guide compares prescribed corticosteroid injections and tablets for adults with arthritis. It does not choose a medicine, dose or taper for you. A new painful joint needs a diagnosis before treatment, especially after an injection.

  • A suddenly very painful, swollen or hot joint needs urgent assessment. Contact an urgent GP service or NHS 111 now, particularly if you cannot move the joint, cannot bear weight or feel unwell. Fever is not always present in septic arthritis. Do not wait a week or assume that worsening heat and pain after an injection is an expected reaction.
  • Call 999 for a serious allergic reaction: sudden swelling of the mouth, tongue or throat, struggling to breathe, or collapse. Infection with new confusion, very fast breathing or blue, pale or blotchy skin can be sepsis and also needs emergency help. Do not drive yourself to A&E.
  • If you have adrenal insufficiency or have been told you are at risk, follow your emergency plan. Sudden severe illness, collapse or marked drowsiness may be an adrenal crisis: call 999. If you have a prescribed emergency steroid injection and training, use it as instructed and still call 999.

NHS 111 is an urgent-advice route in England, Scotland and Wales. In Northern Ireland use your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Use 999 for an emergency throughout the UK.

The route matters: not all injections are local

Corticosteroids reduce inflammation. They are different from anabolic steroids. The useful comparison is where the medicine acts, not simply a needle versus a tablet.

  • Into a joint or nearby soft tissue: an intra-articular or peri-articular injection aims to treat a particular painful area. Some medicine can still enter the bloodstream; local does not mean risk-free.
  • Into a muscle: an intramuscular steroid injection can have a wider, whole-body effect. It is not the same as a small targeted joint injection and shares important systemic risks.
  • Tablets, often prednisolone: these act throughout the body and may be used when inflammation affects several joints or as part of a specialist treatment plan. A tablet course is not automatically the right alternative when a joint injection is unsuitable.

The preparation, dose, condition and your other medicines matter. Ask which steroid and route are being offered, what benefit is realistic, and what happens if it does not work.

Osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis need different plans

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends considering an intra-articular corticosteroid injection when other medicines are ineffective or unsuitable, or to support therapeutic exercise. NICE describes short-term relief of 2 to 10 weeks. This is not a guarantee that it will work or a promise of months of relief. The aim may be to make movement and rehabilitation more manageable; an injection does not reverse osteoarthritis.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE supports short-term glucocorticoids for flares and considering a short bridging course when starting a new conventional DMARD. Oral, intramuscular and intra-articular routes can each have a place. Steroids do not replace a plan to control the underlying inflammatory disease.

Long-term steroids are not a routine goal in rheumatoid arthritis, but saying they are never used is too simple. NICE allows continuation in established rheumatoid arthritis only after long-term complications have been discussed and all other treatment options have been offered. If you already take them long term, ask for a treatment review, not an abrupt stop.

What to expect after a local injection

The time to benefit varies with the preparation and problem being treated. Arthritis UK explains that some injections work within hours and others take around a week. If a local anaesthetic is included, early numbness or pain relief may wear off before the steroid takes effect. That early change does not prove whether the steroid will help.

A temporary increase in pain can occur after an injection. However, a joint becoming increasingly hot and painful, particularly with illness, needs immediate medical advice rather than being labelled a harmless flare. Follow the urgent section above.

Get written aftercare for the actual joint and procedure: when to rest, return to work, drive, lift or restart exercise. NHS hydrocortisone advice describes resting the joint for 24 hours and avoiding heavy exercise; Arthritis UK cautions against overdoing activity for the first two weeks. These are not interchangeable instructions for every injection. Follow your injector's plan and ask if it is unclear. Feeling numb or suddenly better is not permission to overload the area.

Risks to discuss before choosing either route

Local injections can cause bruising, pain, skin colour changes or thinning of skin and underlying tissue. Joint infection is rare but serious. Repeated injections in the same area may damage tissues. There is no personal safe repeat-injection allowance in this article: agree the interval, total exposure and review point with the clinician.

Tablets and systemic injections can cause sleep disturbance, appetite or mood changes and indigestion, including during a short course. Higher doses and longer exposure increase risks such as infection, high blood sugar, high blood pressure, osteoporosis, eye problems and adrenal suppression. A local injection can also raise blood sugar and, especially with repeated doses or other steroids, affect adrenal function. A short course or local route does not guarantee no side effects.

Tell the clinician about diabetes, current infection or antibiotics, recent injections, all other steroid medicines, osteoporosis or fractures, eye disease, previous serious mood problems, planned surgery and vaccinations. Bring a complete medicine list, including inhalers, creams and over-the-counter medicines. Do not stop anticoagulants such as warfarin yourself to prepare for an injection. Ask a pharmacist before adding ibuprofen, naproxen or another NSAID to prednisolone.

If you have diabetes, agree who will check glucose after treatment and what readings or symptoms need help. Report new eyesight changes or major mood changes promptly. Thoughts of self-harm need urgent mental-health help; if you cannot keep yourself safe or there is immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E.

Tablets need a clear finish, taper and illness plan

Take the exact course on your prescription. NHS prednisolone advice says not to stop without speaking to a doctor: the dose may need to fall gradually to avoid withdrawal or a return of the condition. Not every short course needs a taper, but the decision depends on your treatment history and risk. Do not copy another person's schedule, restart leftovers or reduce the dose because an injection has helped.

Ask whether you need a blue steroid treatment card, a red NHS Steroid Emergency Card, or both. If issued, carry them and show them before emergency care, surgery or other procedures. Include recent injections when discussing your total steroid exposure.

If you have, or are at high risk of, adrenal insufficiency, get written sick-day rules and emergency instructions before you are ill. Vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can prevent absorption of oral steroids. NICE guidance says people with adrenal insufficiency who cannot absorb oral glucocorticoids during illness need hospital treatment. Follow your emergency plan and seek immediate medical help, not a routine appointment. Do not invent a dose increase from this guide.

Questions to leave the appointment with

  • What is the diagnosis and target of treatment: one area or wider inflammation?
  • What improvement should I expect, by when, and when will we review it?
  • What are my aftercare, glucose-monitoring and infection-warning instructions?
  • If I take tablets, what is the exact finish or taper plan, and do I need steroid cards or sick-day rules?
  • If this keeps recurring, does the longer-term arthritis treatment need changing?

Read the leaflet for your particular medicine and ask your clinician or pharmacist about anything unclear. General UK educational information, not an individual treatment plan. Living With Arthritis is independent of Arthritis UK. A fresh qualified clinical review of this revision is pending.

key_takeaways: A joint injection is targeted, but a muscle injection can act throughout the body. Neither route is risk-free.
A suddenly very painful or hot swollen joint needs urgent assessment, even without fever. Do not wait a week after an injection.
Get written aftercare and, for tablets, a finish or taper plan. Ask about steroid cards and sick-day rules where relevant.
